items.body: A "Stop Prop 1" sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, held at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1, the ballot initiative that sought to legalize abortion in the state up to fetal viability or in emergencies, and would have enumerated rights to other types of reproductive healthcare. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. Wednesday. The voter-led ballot initiative received 43.68% of the vote, or 286,909 votes in the 2026 general election, as of 2:37 a.m. on Wednesday. More than 56.32% voted against it, early results showed. The proposition needed a simple majority of votes to pass. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the group formed to author and support the initiative, conceded that it did not pass in a press release sent just after 12:20 a.m. Idahoans United for Women and Families Executive Director Melanie Folwell speaks about Proposition 1 at the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings rally at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Jim Max for the Idaho Capital Sun) “This is a tremendous, frankly gutting, loss, especially for the women, families, and physicians of Idaho,” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families, said in a press release. “We will see more doctors leave the state as a result of this election. And, most urgently, women will continue to suffer needlessly under one of the most cruel abortion bans in the nation.” Election officials were still counting ballots early into Wednesday morning. Idaho’s election results do not become official until they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24. The initiative would’ve repealed Idaho’s strict abortion ban, which outlaws nearly all abortions, except to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester when a police report is provided. Idaho’s ban carries felony prison sentences and licensing penalties for doctors who perform abortions outside of the exemptions, as well as possible civil lawsuits for a minimum of $20,000. Opponents of the ballot initiative argue that it is the state’s prerogative to protect fetuses’ lives, and that Idaho’s exemptions are sufficient to protect the mother’s life. The Idaho GOP, the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise strongly opposed the initiative. Opponents formed a group called Stop Prop 1 in response to the proposed initiative. “The people of Idaho have spoken,” Stop Prop 1 communications director Mary Strow said in a press release. “They saw through the smokescreen of deception and barrage of out-of-state funded ads that sought to rewrite our laws and reshape our values. Idaho is and will always be a state that values life and protects the unborn.” Idahoans United for Women and Families formed in 2024 to explore ways to restore abortion access in the state in response to the U.S. Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022, which triggered Idaho’s bans. Idahoans United in July turned in nearly 110,000 signatures to the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office to qualify for the 2026 general election ballot. In Idaho, to qualify for the general election, supporters must collect signatures from at least 6% of the registered voters statewide and from at least 6% of the registered voters in at least 18 of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. To achieve the 6% statewide total, supporters needed 70,725 verified signatures. Its supporters argued Idaho’s laws were overreaching and potentially dangerous for pregnant women, and led to the state losing OB-GYNs. The petition to get the initiative on the ballot included signatures from Idaho voters across party lines . Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. The AP called the elections for Idaho’s Congressional District 1 at 9:43 p.m. Tuesday for incumbent U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher, at the Congressional District 2 race for U.S. Rep. Jim Risch in the general election. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Independent challenger Todd Achilles trailed with 33.5%, followed by independent Natalie Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby with 6.89% and 2.87%, respectively. Risch, 86, is in his third, six-year term in the U.S. Senate. He is chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and serves on the Energy and Natural Resources, Small Business and Entrepreneurship, Intelligence, and Ethics committees. He was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 2008. “Thank you to every Idahoan who placed their trust in me to continue serving our great state in the United States Senate,” Risch said in an emailed statement. “Representing Idaho is the honor of my life, and I am proud to fight for the people and values that make our state special.” Achilles, 58, is a former Democratic state legislator from Boise who left the party and Statehouse seat to run for the U.S. Senate as an independent in 2025. His campaign out-raised any recent U.S. Senate challenger in Idaho, collecting more than $1.8 million. During the campaign, Achilles publicly promised to not caucus with either party if elected, and to resign after two terms. Risch’s closest general election contest for U.S. Senate was in 2008, when he won with 57.7% against Democratic former Congressman Larry LaRocco, independent Rex Rammell, Libertarian Kent Marmon, and the independent candidate who legally changed his name to Pro-Life, according to the Idaho Secretary of State elections database. He was followed by Democrat Kaylee Peterson, who had 28.55% of the vote, and independent Sarah Zabel with 6.02%. Constitution Party candidate Brendan Gomez had .9% of the vote. items.body: Idaho Gov. Brad Little speaks to supporters at a Republican election night watch party at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little was reelected in Tuesday’s general election and will serve a third term as the Gem State’s governor, according to the Associated Press. All other Republican candidates for statewide office were also reelected. The Associated Press called the race for Little at 10:36 p.m. Tuesday. Little addressed his supporters and several Republican officials at a downtown Boise convention hall at about 10:20 p.m. Mountain time Tuesday night, shortly before the race was officially called. “I’m humbled to have your support, grateful for your confidence, and proud to have the opportunity to continue to serve this great state,” Little told supporters Tuesday night. “Tonight’s decision results send a clear message: Idahoans want to keep moving forward. They believe in the direction the state is headed. They believe in Idaho values, and they rightfully expect us to keep delivering.” Little, a Republican from Emmett, was projected to beat his two closest challengers, Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner. As of 2:06 a.m. Mountain time Wednesday, Little had received 369,360 votes, or 57.3%, while Pickens was in second place with 206,218 votes, or 32%. Stegner was in third place, with 49,279 votes, or 7.6%. Several other candidates ran for governor as well. Libertarian Paul Sand received 10,377 votes, or 1.6%. A Constitution Party candidate who changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life received 8,649 votes, or 1.3%. And an independent named Jacob Burnett ran as a write-in candidate and had received 227 votes. Little will serve his third, four-year term as Idaho’s governor. He was first elected governor in 2018, having previously served as lieutenant governor and a member of the Idaho Senate. In addition to Little, each of Idaho’s statewide incumbent Republican officials was also leading their re-election bids Tuesday night, according to partial unofficial election results released Tuesday by the state. The Associated Press also called the race for Idaho secretary of state in favor of Republican Secretary of State Phil McGrane at 10:31 p.m. Wednesday. Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke, Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf, Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth and Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield won their re-election bids as well. Idaho Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke leads Democrat Eric Myricks Idaho’s lieutenant governor serves as president of the Idaho Senate but only votes in cases of a tie vote. The lieutenant governor also serves as acting governor while the governor is out of the state or unable to perform the duties of office. Bedke, a Republican from Oakley, held a large lead over Democratic challenger Eric Myricks of Nampa. As of 2:05 a.m. Wednesday, Bedke has received 403,994 votes, or 63.7%. Myricks had received 229,536 votes, or 36.2%. Bedke is running for his second four-year term as lieutenant governor. He previously served as the longtime speaker of the Idaho House of Representatives. items.body: U.S. Sen. Frank Church, D-Idaho, (left) stands next to Idaho Gov. Cecil Andrus in 1975. (Photo courtesy of the Special Collections and Archives, Albertsons Library, Boise State University) Idahoans are encouraged to participate in a two-day event this week that honors the environmental and political legacy of Cecil Andrus, Idaho’s longest-serving governor. Share your ‘Cece story’: Boise State’s Andrus Center will host ‘History Harvest’ for book project The Andrus for Idaho: History Harvest event, hosted by the Boise State University Andrus Center, includes several panel discussions and presentations from some of the people who knew Andrus best, as well as an “Antiques Roadshow”-style History Harvest, which encourages Idahoans to bring in photos, memorabilia, artifacts, letters and oral histories from Andrus’ time in office to have them documented and archived. The two-day event will begin at 9 a.m. Friday and 9:45 a.m. Saturday at SPACE in Boise State University’s Albertsons Library, 1865 Friendship Lane on BSU’s campus. Both days of the event will go through the afternoon, and the public can join the activities at anytime throughout the day. The Andrus Center is also looking for volunteers to help with the event, including set-up beforehand, guiding visitors and helping at informational stations during the event and tear down and archival work afterward. To register as a volunteer, fill out this Google form online . Who was Cecil Andrus? Cecil Andrus, the last Democrat to serve as Idaho’s governor, died at age 85 in 2017. He was the only person to serve four terms – a nonconsecutive 14 years – as Idaho governor. But his service to the state and nation extended far beyond that one role. After serving in the U.S. Navy during the Korean War, he was concerned about the direction of Idaho’s public schools and ran for the state Senate in 1960 at just 28 years old, winning the seat. That began a longtime tenure in state politics, with his first stint as Idaho governor from 1971-1977. Serving as governor would eventually help prepare him for his role as U.S. secretary of the Interior in the Jimmy Carter administration from 1977-1981. He again was elected Idaho governor from 1987-1995. As Idaho’s population changes and grows, Emily Wakild, the Cecil D. Andrus endowed chairwoman for environment and public lands in the School of the Environment, College of Arts and Sciences, said the event is a way to bring the state’s history to life — and to capture the memories and items related to Andrus’ political life before it’s too late. Volunteers will be on-hand to scan photos, letters and other documents, while others will be available to record oral histories and personal stories about Andrus. That itself articulates, I think, some of the really strong values of the Andrus Center, which are public dialog, public interaction with lots of different perspectives and public ideas about moving forward.” Many of the people who worked with Andrus are aging, and organizers of the event hope to capture a more contextual picture of Andrus and his politics before they pass on, Wakild said. “We especially want to get people that do have those memories,” Wakild said. “But we also want people that have been here 10 minutes — people that can say, ‘oh, I moved here. items.body: Walking from one end of Meridian Technical Charter High to the other takes only about two minutes, as the entire building is only 19,000 square feet. However, within the 14 classrooms, students are learning curricula that could be taught at university level. Last week, Idaho Legislators joined representatives from the Idaho Charter School Association to tour Meridian Technical Charter High School (MTCHS) and Meridian Medical Arts Charter High School (MMACHS). After the tours, they sat for panels with students and parents. The schools are two different buildings that share the same campus. They both set students up for success after high school, but their specialties couldn’t be more different. At Meridian Technical Charter High School, students take introductory coding and networking lessons their freshman year. MTCHS is focused on providing a progressive, technical education experience. Apart from a regular academic course load, the school provides students with over 1,000 hours of technical training and specific training in personal and workplace skills. There are six different pathways with various focus areas provided at the school, including Computer, Networking, Media, Web, Software, and Electronics. MTCHS accepts only freshmen by a lottery due to the rigorous 4-year curriculum plan that starts with a rotation of the different pathways. At the end of their first year, they must choose one pathway to continue with until graduation. “If they don’t come in as a freshman, they’re so far behind because they start taking certifications their sophomore year,” said Craig Miller, Principal of MTCHS. Industry certifications are a big part of MTCHS. The school provides over 20 certifications in things such as Adobe, JavaScript, Intuit QuickBooks, and more. In the Business Capstone class, students combine their tech skills with entrepreneurship skills by working on large business projects that benefit their community. In an IT class, students are responding to Computer Help Desk Tickets that have been sent from around the school. The Graphic Design Classroom at MTCHS. items.body: Idaho Conservation League Executive Director Courtney Washburn Experienced conservationist and policy leader Courtney Washburn has been named the new executive director of the Idaho Conservation League, the league and its board of directors announced last month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Washburn succeeds previous Executive Director Justin Hayes, who announced last year he was taking a new position at the group American Rivers. The Idaho Conservation League is a more than 50-year-old nonprofit organization with a mission to protect clean air, clean water, land and wildlife. The new role represents a homecoming for Washburn, who previously served as the Idaho Conservation League’s community conservation director and statehouse lobbyist from 2006 to 2015. In her new role, Washburn is focusing on connecting and partnering with people and groups to take on the challenges of protecting Idaho. “I’m really focused on both growing the conservation community and connecting – or reconnecting, depending on how long people have lived in Idaho – with the conservation values and the actions that’s needed to protect this great state,” Washburn said in an interview Wednesday. “Progress would be to finally dispel the myth that people who care about conservation are associated with one party or another,” Washburn said. “I’d really like to see a durable kind of big tent. Everyone has a voice to speak up for their values, whether it be clean air, clean water, public lands.” “People care deeply about their state, and if you get to the core values, there are far less arguments, in my experience,” she added. Washburn also previously served as executive director for Conservation Voters for Idaho from 2015 to 2020. More recently, Washburn served as chief of staff for the city of Boise from 2020 to 2026, where she directed municipal operations, longterm planning and climate initiatives. Boise Dev reported in May that Boise Mayor Lauren McLean authorized a large severance payment for Washburn after Washburn left the city position. items.body: The Snake River runs through Idaho Falls. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho has periodically faced serious threats to its water sovereignty from an overreaching federal government. In the early 1950s, when Len Jordan was Idaho governor, the feds wanted to build a massive dam on the Snake River in Hells Canyon. That would have usurped Idaho control of its upstream waters. Jordan stopped the proposal, opting instead for the three existing Idaho Power company dams in order to protect Idaho’s control of those waters. The next water fight occurred after I was elected as Idaho attorney general in 1982. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights Idaho Power had just received an erroneous decision from the Idaho Supreme Court, giving the company practical control of Snake River waters above its Swan Falls Dam in Ada County. Gov. John Evans and I were able to work together behind the scenes and across the political aisle to defeat that threat. When we were able to get the conflict settled to the state’s advantage, the next federal threat raised its ugly head. In December 1987, Congress was on the verge of approving legislation that would have given the feds the ability to control the flow of Snake River waters above Deer Flats Wildlife Refuge in Canyon County. The matter was being handled behind closed doors in congressional offices. When my staff members learned that a political deal was being made to compromise the state’s interests, I blew the whistle, the Idaho water community erupted in anger, and the threat was brought to a screeching halt. Anyone interested in the details can check out pages 337-345 of my book on the subject – “ A Little Dam Problem .” The latest threat to Idaho’s water sovereignty surfaced less than two months ago. Shortly after it was announced that the Idaho National Laboratory had been selected as a finalist for designation as a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus , the Trump administration launched an extremely troubling lawsuit challenging Idaho’s ability to “administer” the federal water right at the INL. In practical terms it means that, if there is a water shortage involving water rights in the INL vicinity, any reduction or mitigation would fall wholly upon the shoulders of other Idaho water users — farmers, fish producers and other folks dependent on those waters. The INL would be exempt. Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming ‘supremacy’ over our water is a gut punch to all Idahoans The lawsuit was filed against Idaho in the federal court in Boise on Sept. 11, without any attendant publicity from either side. While the allegations focus primarily upon the INL water right, the complaint seeks much broader relief. The Trump administration wants “a declaration that the Idaho Department of Water Resources lacks the authority to administer federal water rights” and “an order permanently enjoining the Director of IDWR from exercising his authority” under any state law as to the United States or its agencies. In short, the administration is asking the court to prevent Idaho from administering federal water rights anywhere within state borders. This is wholly without precedent and contrary to the determination of rights in the Snake River Basin Adjudication . The agreement settling the Swan Falls water right fight called for filing a case in state court to adjudicate all water rights to Snake River Basin waters. That is, to quantify and prioritize those rights in court proceedings. Idaho specifically sought and received approval to include all federal water rights under a federal law, called the McCarran Amendment, that permits federal claims to be determined in a state court adjudication. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026. items.body: Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026. A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote the ballot measure days before the election. In an opinion released late Friday night , Judge Davis VanderVelde found the ads did not violate Idaho campaign finance laws and declined to keep them from being broadcast by local stations. A Republican Party operative and three board members of Too Extreme for Idaho, which opposes restoring abortion rights under Prop 1, filed their lawsuit Tuesday morning . They said the scheme used by Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), the Idaho Democratic Party and its gubernatorial candidate, Terri Pickens, concealed the true origin of who paid for the ads. IUWF, which qualified Prop 1 for the ballot, gave the Idaho Democratic Party more than $720,000 in recent weeks. The party then purchased advertising through Pickens’ campaign. All political candidates receive significant discounts on ads in the 60 days leading up to an election compared to political groups. “Ultimately, Plaintiffs’ assertion that the monies from IUWF were specifically contributed for support of Proposition 1 with the intent of concealing the original donor for such advertisements requires logical leaps that are not fully supported by the evidence,” VanderVelde wrote. Each of these transactions is publicly available in the state’s campaign finance database, which the plaintiffs cited in the evidence presented to the judge. VanderVelde said there’s also no evidence showing that IUWF still controlled the hundreds of thousands of dollars it donated to the state Democratic Party. An attorney for the defendants argued in court Thursday that the party had the final say in how any of that money was spent, which VanderVelde said was not proven otherwise by the plaintiffs. “The Court recognizes that the parties have had a short time to advance this lawsuit and that if there was additional time, additional facts may be developed by either party which could lend further credence to their claims or defenses,” he wrote. That said, the judge found there may still be outstanding legal questions about whether the ads are truly for a candidate or a proposition and whether the lower rates should apply. “However, without further law or authority significant questions remain as to what constitutes an appropriate advertisement under the law in order to qualify as an advertisement promoting a candidate.” Tom Luna, one of the plaintiffs, released a statement saying he and the three other men who brought the lawsuit disagree with the decision, but that it was important voters know who paid for the ads. “I’m sure many voters are as mad as I am about these dirty tricks. Let’s make sure we turn our frustration into action by showing up on Election Day, making our voices heard, and standing for life,” Luna said. A request for comment from the Idaho Democratic Party wasn’t immediately returned late Friday night. Memorandum Decision and Order Denying Motion For Prelimiary Injunction

Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. Seyb’s challenge, which argued Idaho’s abortion ban’s lack of exemptions to prevent serious harm to the mother’s health or death from self-harm were unconstitutional, will continue to be litigated in court. Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan said in the majority opinion that Seyb’s argument for a constitutional right to abortion as a health-saving measure or in cases of risk of self-harm were unlikely to align with the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which overturned Roe v. Wade. “We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” the majority decision said. “… Idaho has a strong interest in limiting abortions to those allowed under its law. This interest clearly outweighs the potential harm to Dr. Seyb of having to abide by Idaho’s law pending the resolution of this appeal.” Wardlaw concurred with the majority decision. Judge Marsha S. Berzon disagreed, writing that the high court’s decision only applied to elective abortions, and not when the procedure may be medically necessary or indicated. Berzon agreed with district court Judge B. Lynn Winmill, whose previous order argued there was likely a “fundamental right” to abortions to preserve the mother’s health. Berzon also argued that the risk of harm for Seyb’s patients was greater than that of the state’s. “… with the stay imposed by the majority in place, some women with serious pregnancy complications will during the pendency of this appeal be required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health,” Berzon wrote. “The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury.” Seyb said in a written statement, “Laws that criminalize abortion make pregnancy less safe.” “I will continue to advocate for the right of every patient to make important medical decisions without government interference,” he said. The conservative Christian advocacy group the Idaho Family Policy Center, which helped author Idaho’s abortion ban allowing civil lawsuits against doctors, celebrated Friday’s decision in a press release. “Pregnant mothers don’t have a constitutional right to abortion merely because they threaten to harm themselves,” Idaho Family Policy Center Blaine Conzatti said in the release. “Women in mental health crises need treatment, not abortion. This decision ensures that our pro-life laws here in Idaho will continue protecting both mother and baby.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.body: In a rare but legally required move, the Canyon County Board of County Commissioners on Thursday appointed naturopathic medical doctor Brett Butterfield to fill a vacancy on the Vallivue school board. If a school board in Idaho fails to fill a vacancy within 120 days, the local county commissioners are required to make the appointment. Trustee Toni Brinegar resigned on June 9, which was 142 days ago as of Thursday. “This is a statutory requirement,” Canyon County Chief Civil Deputy Aaron Bazzoli told the commissioners at Thursday’s meeting. He said the school district provided Butterfield’s name, but there were “some issues with how they went about the process.” Commissioner Leslie Van Beek thanked Bazzoli for putting on the record the county’s statutory authority to make the appointment. “I don’t know that the board has been asked — not in my tenure — to be the one that appoints a person for a vacancy on a school board,” she said. She then made a motion to appoint Butterfield. “We’re not here to overstep the wishes of the Vallivue school board,” Van Beek said. “For whatever reason, they had problems, so this was the name that surfaced as the candidate they wanted to fill that seat and I am in favor.” With the appointment secured, the five-member Vallivue school board is now back to full strength after two resignations this summer. After signing a new contract this summer that includes $20,000 annual raises over the next three years, Bub will take home $250,822 this school year. The second-highest salary belongs to Wendy Johnson, superintendent of the Boise School District, who will earn $219,454. Her predecessor, Lisa Roberts, who retired last school year, earned $218,362 . West Ada is the state’s largest school district with more than 37,300 students. Boise is the second-largest district with nearly 22,000 students. The state’s largest districts tend to have the highest-paid superintendents, but that’s not always the case. The Blaine County School District is the 26th largest in the state. items.body: The Snake River flows alongside the Idaho Falls greenbelt. (Photo courtesy of Hyo Lee/U.S. Department of Energy) Throughout history there has been one thing all Idahoans agreed on — water is the lifeblood of Idaho. Water has made our southern Idaho sagebrush country bloom with farms and ranches, and water has been crucial for the protection of our wildlife and our outdoor way of life. Protecting Idaho’s water rights from outside threats has been an article of faith — almost a religion — and any attempt by outsiders to get their hands on our water has been fighting words for all Idaho politicians regardless of political party or persuasion. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights That’s why the Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming “supremacy” over Idaho’s water serving the Idaho National Laboratory is a gut punch to the people of Idaho. But our current political leaders, unlike those throughout history, have played a role in giving the Trump administration the notion that Idaho is a lap dog for whatever the president wants by their silence and eagerness to partner with the federal government regardless of the consequences for Idahoans, their economy and their way of life. Last summer, without informing the people of Idaho, Gov. Brad Little signed a memorandum of understanding with the Trump administration hoping that the Idaho National Laboratory could become a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and accept 33 percent of all radioactive waste generated in the country . Little has not explained how this campus and taking the waste will affect our precious water supply nor how it will impact the Snake River Aquifer, which supplies a significant amount of water to our southern Idaho farms, ranches, trout farms and cities. Other than a few comments for a story published by the Idaho Capital Sun , the governor has said little about how this major initiative will affect Idaho. Our congressional delegation has also remained silent on this issue except to say the campus will bring economic prosperity and jobs to eastern Idaho. Now, through the lawsuit the Trump administration has filed in U.S. District Court, we know that the federal government views the water it receives from Idaho as its water and that Idaho has no legal right to curtail water to INL even during one of the worse drought seasons in the state’s history. The Trump administration argues that federal installations like INL are “shielded by the supremacy clause” from state regulations unless “Congress has provided clear and unambiguous authorization for such regulation.” The Trump administration also argues, as it has while promoting the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and the radioactive waste repository, that Idaho’s decision to curtail INL’s water has “safety, economic and energy consequences.” Moreover, the Trump administration says that “curtailment of INL’s water right would disrupt this national nuclear energy momentum,” another way of saying it would disrupt President Trump’s quest to build nuclear reactors across the country. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) One Boise State. Five priorities. David Hahn formally began his presidency Thursday afternoon — with a call for “shared purpose” and an outline of commitments to the Boise State University community and the state. Hahn’s list of priorities includes an ambitious fundraising drive, and enhanced partnerships with Idaho employers. “One Boise State begins with our students, faculty, and staff,” Hahn said at a ceremony marking his investiture as Boise State’s eighth president. “But it extends far beyond campus.” A president’s investiture is steeped in academic tradition, and Hahn’s ceremony was steeped in Bronco culture — with performances by a Boise State choral ensemble and the Blue Thunder Marching Band, and an unannounced cameo from football coach Spencer Danielson. Thursday’s ceremony also came nearly four months into Hahn’s actual presidency; the State Board of Education hired Hahn on July 1 , bringing a turbulent 16-month job search to a conclusion. But Hahn leveraged the moment, and used a 17-minute speech, to hammer home the “one Boise State” theme. He also articulated his five goals: student success; preparing graduates for the workforce; university research; philanthropy and athletics. Hahn’s to-do list contained at least one new wrinkle. He pledged to build on Boise State’s $500 million Unbridled fundraising campaign, setting a new $700 million target with an emphasis on student opportunities, research and endowed dean’s positions. “We can do that, together,” he said. Boise State hit the $500 million target in 2025 , and Unbridled has now raised $565 million. Hahn — who came to Boise State from the University of Arizona, where he served as dean of the college of engineering — restated his commitment to research. He again pledged to pursue top-tier R1 research status through the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education, a designation that could bring more research funding to the university. He also said Boise State should put its research to work “to power and protect” Idaho. Hahn also said Boise State needs to work closely with Idaho businesses from high-tech to healthcare, with a focus on hands-on learning and internships. “Our responsibility is to prepare the next generation of talent.” Hahn doubled down on athletics. Weeks after the State Board of Education gave Boise State athletics the go-ahead to run on an $18 million deficit — and use other university funds to make up the gap — Hahn called sports an essential part of the university’s mission. Hahn said Boise State can build one of the nation’s premier athletic programs, even in a turbulent time for intercollegiate sports . “Boise State will not sit on the sidelines and wait for someone else to determine our future,” Hahn said. But Hahn said his first commitment — and his highest priority — is student success. And Hahn began his speech with a shoutout to the ceremony’s opening speaker: Ramiro Mendoza, a Boise State junior majoring in marketing. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) It took two years for Chrissy Teigen to realize she’d had an abortion and not a miscarriage, longer to understand what went wrong in her pregnancy, and not until this week to realize she hadn’t fully grappled with it emotionally. Teigen, a former model and business owner, came to Idaho on Wednesday to make a final push leading up to Nov. 3 in favor of Proposition 1, the ballot measure that would restore access to abortion in Idaho. The state has a near-total ban that applies to any stage of pregnancy, with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. The initiative, if passed, would also protect access to birth control and fertility assistance treatments such as in vitro fertilization. Opponents to the measure have called the initiative too extreme because it would allow abortions up to fetal viability, which was the law in Idaho prior to the ban, with exceptions after that point when the pregnancy threatens a patient’s health or life. Prior to a rally in downtown Boise with Prop 1 volunteers and supporters, Teigen — who lived in Idaho Falls in the early 1990s — met privately at a coffee shop with 12 Idaho women who have been telling their stories for the campaign about needing abortion care in Idaho. The women sat in a circle and told brief versions of their stories: miscarriages that led to septic infections because of hesitant medical providers, travel out of state for fatal anomalies and catastrophic health complications, and memorials to the babies they lost. Nonprofit organization Idahoans United for Women and Families, which has led the campaign for the initiative, coordinated the event, and owners of Neckar Coffee donated the space and coffee. Kate Campbell spoke of her son, Remy, and the infected placenta that caused her water to break at 20 weeks and begin labor. A fetus generally can’t survive outside of the womb before 22 weeks, and every day that goes by without an abortion procedure increases the risk of a potentially life-threatening infection, which can cause organ damage and lead to fertility loss. Since Idaho’s law only allows for intervention to save a patient’s life, doctors decided not to wait until she was close to death and airlifted Campbell to Utah for care. Utah allows abortion until 18 weeks, and after that, the law includes an exception to preserve a patient’s health, not just to prevent death. “The only ‘cure,’ if you will, for an infected placenta is giving birth,” Campbell said through tears. She now has a 14-month-old daughter. Rebecca Crozier and other Idaho women sit side-by-side across from Chrissy Teigen to tell their stories of needing abortion care and being unable to access it in their home state because of the near-total ban. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) Desi Ballis had a similar story about a virus she contracted early in pregnancy that caused a fatal anomaly that also put her health in danger. A doctor at her 20-week ultrasound told her she needed to get to Utah as quickly as possible, and she and her husband, Morgan, made the five-hour drive and called multiple hospitals and clinics before they found someone who could help. “It was just horrific,” Ballis said. Others included Rebecca Crozier, who received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly at 11 weeks and told Stateline her story this week, and Abby Nichols , who traveled to Seattle for an abortion after she received a fetal diagnosis of Trisomy 18, a chromosomal abnormality that is often fatal or life-limiting. (Idaho State photo) Idaho’s colleges and universities didn’t step off the enrollment cliff. However, student numbers dropped this fall, for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic. The small decrease — fewer than 600 students, across the state’s eight colleges and universities — is still a warning sign. Especially for Idaho policymakers, who will make it easier — or tougher — for the state’s higher education system to compete in a cutthroat environment. A ‘mini-cliff?’ What the numbers say First, here are the raw stats: fall student headcount at the eight colleges and universities. 2021 2025 2026 One-year change Boise State University 25,793 28,461 28,476 +0.05% Idaho State University 12,157 13,910 13,533 -2.7% University of Idaho 11,303 12,383 12,275 -0.8% Lewis-Clark State College 3,710 4,037 3,892 -3.5% College of Western Idaho 10,448 11,724 11,626 -0.8% College of Southern Idaho 8,148 10,545 10,435 -1.0% North Idaho College 4,579 4,662 4,833 +3.6% College of Eastern Idaho 2,157 3,351 3,406 +1.6% Total 78,295 89,073 88,476 -0.7% And here’s some perspective on that one-year, 0.7% decrease. Fall enrollment last decreased in 2020, during the heart of the pandemic. That year, Idaho colleges and universities lost more than 4,100 students, a 5.2% decrease. (For more backstory, here’s our in-depth 2021 series on the COVID enrollment crunch .) (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) Enrollment began to rebound in the fall of 2021, and the numbers have generally kept growing ever since. At every college and university in Idaho — including the five schools reporting an enrollment decrease this fall — student numbers are ahead of where they were five years ago. The 2020 dropoff had an obvious cause: a global health crisis. This year? It’s not quite as straightforward. “It’s too early to point to a single cause, and our research team is continuing to examine the underlying trends,” State Board of Education Executive Director Jennifer White said in a statement to EdNews Wednesday. Their worries center on declining birth rates — a trend rooted in the housing bubble that triggered the Great Recession. Fewer babies translate, eventually, into fewer college-aged young adults. The U.S. housing crisis reached its crescendo in 2007 and 2008 . That should mean fewer college-aged students, starting right about now. If you haven’t mailed your ballot yet, election officials encourage you to physically drop off your absentee ballot in-person at an election office or drop box. Even though the president isn’t on the ballot this year, it’s still a big election year for Idaho. All statewide offices — such as the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state superintendent, state controller and state treasurer — are up for grabs, along with three congressional seats in the U.S. House and Senate, and all 105 state legislative seats. So are local races like for county commissioners, highway district officials and even a runoff election for an Ada County judge. But perhaps the biggest race this year is Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights. That’s one of several ballot measures that voters can decide on, along with a proposed constitutional amendment that would allow only the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun. items.body: If you distrust government with spending and tax decisions, why would you put politicians at your state capitol in charge of more of it? That’s the question at the center of Idaho’s current debate over property taxes. There is no statewide property tax in Idaho, but local governments can collect property tax revenue. Property taxes frustrate homeowners for understandable reasons. Paying off your mortgage does not end the annual bill. A rising home value does not put cash in your checking account. For retirees and families with tight budgets, the burden can be substantial. But property taxes in Idaho are a creature of local government: schools, fire departments, cities, sewer, etc. In many cases, local voters have approved the new taxes and fees collected. If you’ve voted in favor of a bond, levy, or other local tax measure, you are partly responsible for the extra rate you might be paying. There are various ideas on how to eliminate the local property tax burden, but all of them have drawbacks. For example, we examined the concept of doing away with property taxes and, in exchange, giving local governments the option to adopt limited sales taxes. The concept is that this spreads the burden and allows visitors to cover part of the burden. It might work well in some areas but would likely be a burden too heavy to handle in others. It wasn’t a proposal; it was a thought experiment. Others have suggested you can do away with local property taxes by simply having local governments be funded by the state in Boise. In other words, they want state taxpayers to pay for local government decisions. But directing state revenue toward local property tax replacement creates two significant trade-offs: greater dependence on Boise and less room for other state tax reductions (such as the income tax). Today, local elected officials must answer to local voters for their spending and many of the taxes supporting it. The connection is imperfect, but important: Officials who approve spending should face the taxpayers expected to finance it. Under a state-funded replacement system, local officials would increasingly look to the Legislature for revenue. Instead of having to justify spending to local taxpayers, they would lobby for larger distributions from Boise. Local budgets would become more dependent on legislative formulas, negotiations, and priorities. Supporters argue that local control would survive because local officials would still decide how to spend the money. But spending authority is only part of the equation. Whoever controls the funding holds considerable power over the recipient. Future legislatures could also change it. During a downturn, lawmakers would face competing demands from state programs and local governments counting on replacement dollars. Imagine a scenario where your local government leaders are not talking to you about local spending but instead wandering the halls of the state capitol looking for revenue from legislative leaders. That’s a concentration of power that is anything but conservative. We should also carefully examine what this idea would mean for future state tax cuts. After all, the state currently collects income and sales tax revenues. If some of those revenues now have to be used for local government spending, we would likely see fewer, if any, income or sales tax cuts. The dreams some have of a grocery tax abolishment would likely go out the window. This is not to say there are not viable paths forward. Idaho can and should restrain local spending, examine overlapping taxing districts, and adopt Truth in Taxation so officials must clearly disclose and defend proposed property tax increases. Communities could also be allowed to consider voter-approved exchanges of property taxes for local sales taxes. Our study shows that approach would be more feasible in some counties than others. Any exchange should include reasonable rate limits and permanent, dollar-for-dollar reductions in property tax authority

items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at Cathedral of the Rockies in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Trump administration is sending election monitors to Idaho’s largest county on Election Day next week, the state’s top election official confirmed Wednesday. The decision comes as the Justice Department plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors — who the DOJ says are meant to assess local compliance with federal voting rights laws — to all 50 states. That would make for a significantly expanded presence than under the Biden administration, which sent election monitors to 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections, States Newsroom reported. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, an elected Republican, said the U.S. Justice Department notified him and the Ada County Clerk’s Office, which runs the election locally, that there will be two teams in Ada County on Election Day. Ada County Clerk Trent Tripple, also a Republican, said around six election monitors who are local to Idaho will be stationed near polling places — but not inside. In a statement, the Justice Department said its election monitors in Idaho and elsewhere will be “doing the routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.” “All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate,” a spokesperson for the federal agency told the Idaho Capital Sun. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s top election official called deployment ‘routine’ The federal election monitors in Idaho, McGrane said, will be ensuring that voters have access to voting and assisting the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, such as by ensuring polling places are abiding by disability access requirements under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or ADA. McGrane called it a routine measure. He said he last remembered election monitors sent to Idaho under the Obama administration. In this file photo, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) “I’m fairly sure we’ve had it under all (presidential) administrations in some form. I can most clearly remember ADA conversations when Obama was president. But it has been routine in the past,” McGrane said in an interview. The Trump administration’s decision to expand election monitors in states for the midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake, follows recent attempts by the administration to intervene in state election processes , such as to restrict mail-in voting and obtain state voter rolls . That history has left some officials across the country concerned about the expanded election monitoring efforts. But McGrane said he isn’t worried. “I’ve seen the concerns among my peers and others nationally,” he said. “Initially, I wanted to understand and make sure what their mission was. After talking to … the new U.S. Attorney John Shirts … I feel reassured that this is something fairly routine. This is something that we’ve experienced before. And I don’t expect that voters will really even notice that it’s happening.” Tripple said he isn’t worried either. “They’ve done this before. items.body: Rebecca Crozier, 27, of Meridian, Idaho, poses in October 2026 with mementos from her baby, Haven. At 11 weeks, she received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly, and had to travel out of state to terminate the pregnancy because of her state’s near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline) MERIDIAN, Idaho — It didn’t take long for doctors to see that something was amiss with Rebecca Crozier’s pregnancy. At her eight-week ultrasound in 2025, they mentioned a possible neural tube defect, she said, but after some research, she thought it was something that could be managed or treated. “If it was a fixable problem, I was ready to quit my job and full-time care for a disabled child,” said Crozier, who is now 27. “That was something that we were prepared to do.” In the time between the two ultrasounds, she had a dream that she was carrying a baby girl, and she and her husband named her Haven. The couple lived in eastern Idaho at the time, and drove two hours to the Boise area to see the maternal-fetal medicine specialists at St. Luke’s, the state’s largest health system. Now at 11 weeks’ gestation, the specialists told her Haven had anencephaly, which occurs when the brain does not develop normally and the skull is left open, exposing brain tissue to amniotic fluid that causes the tissue to dissolve. It is a fatal condition. Rebecca Crozier takes a photo of her belly during her pregnancy before she and her husband, Kris, were told that the fetus would not survive. (Courtesy of Rebecca Crozier) “She was missing a lot of brain tissue,” Crozier recalled. “They were very clear that this baby will not go home with you. You will not take this baby home. This baby will die in the hospital if the baby survives that long.” In many states, even ones with abortion bans, Crozier would have had the option to terminate the pregnancy. But Idaho’s near-total prohibition includes no exceptions for fatal anomalies. It’s one of 11 states that do not have exceptions for anencephaly or other fatal anomalies. Next Tuesday, Idahoans will vote to determine whether the state’s near-total abortion ban should remain the law. Proposition 1, the title of the citizen-led ballot measure, would restore access to abortion until fetal viability, which was the state law before the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. Idaho is the only state this election cycle with an initiative that would restore access in a state with a ban. In Missouri, voters will consider a different initiative — to reinstate a near-total ban after passing a constitutional amendment in 2024 allowing abortion access until viability. If Idaho’s measure passes, patients like Crozier would no longer have to leave the state for an abortion. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the rate of anencephaly among newborns is about 1 in 10,000, and those babies die within a few hours or days. Most cases end in miscarriage or stillbirth; the fatal birth defect affects about 1 in 1,000 pregnancies. Crozier’s was among them. The state of Idaho has awarded $186 million in federal rural healthcare grants — with more than $20 million going into education-related programs. On Wednesday — three days before the feds’ deadline — state officials announced that the first-year grant process was a wrap. “I’m proud of the work that brought us to this point, and I’m excited to see these investments improve care for Idaho families across our state,” said Sen. Julie VanOrden, R-Pingree, the co-chair of a legislative oversight committee that has reviewed the grant applications. Year One: Some highlights The two biggest education-related awards have been in the works for some time . About $12.5 million will go into a suite of 11 initiatives to encourage rural students to pursue healthcare careers. Most of these programs are co-ops involving multiple colleges and universities. The biggest of the group is a $4.3 million Boise State University-led mobile simulation lab project, designed to bring clinical training into rural communities. The State Board of Education will receive $8 million for graduate medical education — rural fellowships and residencies for medical school graduates. Here’s a look at some other education-related grants: The University of Idaho will receive $2 million to create a statewide chronic disease education network. Idaho State University will receive $2 million for a cognitive care pathway network. The U of I and Eat Smart Idaho will share nearly $1.6 million for chronic disease prevention and cancer screening programs. Another U of I grant, of close to $1.2 million, will go toward a pediatric psychiatric assistance line and mental and behavioral health programs. Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and the Blind will receive nearly $900,000 for a mobile pediatric clinic, which will provide specialized hearing testing in rural Idaho. “For many Idaho families — especially in rural areas — affordable, accessible health care is a real concern,” Gov. Brad Little said in a news release touting the first-year grants. “This investment recognizes those challenges and puts resources where they’re needed most.” Year Two funding: No news yet There was some considerable confusion Wednesday about Idaho’s second-year grant. On Wednesday, as state officials announced the wrapup of their first-year grant program, the Trump administration issued a news release that at least implied an additional $186 million was on its way. “Today, the Trump Administration announced nearly $186 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho,” the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services news release said. However, the release simply referred, again, to the first-year grant, which was awarded in December . Idaho won’t find out about its second-year grant for at least a few more weeks. The federal grants are competitive — meaning funding could increase or decrease based on a state’s first-year track record. That’s why Idaho officials and the legislative oversight committee emphasized the importance of meeting the feds’ reporting requirements and hitting the Oct. 30 grant deadline. Idaho potentially has some unfinished business heading into the second year, on at least two education initiatives. The legislative oversight committee discussed the idea of putting some federal money into the undergraduate end of medical education — subsidizing medical school tuition for Idaho students. The idea came up during a July committee meeting , but it never went anywhere. In September, the committee spiked a $1.2 million program with an education nexus. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) How competitive is the race to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate? It depends which poll you look at. According to a poll released last week by the campaign for Todd Achilles, an independent running for U.S. Senate, Republican incumbent Jim Risch has only a six-point lead over Achilles. Eight percent of voters were undecided, the poll found. The poll buoyed a claim by the Achilles campaign: Victory could be within reach. State Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “That tight margin confirms what we’re hearing in every corner of Idaho: voters are tired of career politicians controlled by their party bosses,” Achilles, 58, said in a statement with the poll’s release on Oct. 23. But the latest poll didn’t ask about support for the other two candidates in the race, which has drawn one of the most active attempts in years at unseating Risch, 83, who’s seeking a fourth, six-year-term. And Risch’s campaign polling — featuring the full line up of candidates — shows him pummeling Achilles. In the run up to Election Day in a state without much independent polling, that’s the sort of divide in polling outcomes that some pollsters expect voters to see. “Usually about this time, the candidates or the campaigns for ballot issues are publishing polls that show you that they’re going to win,” Stuart Elway, a longtime independent pollster in Washington state, said in an interview. In Idaho, independent political polls — which aren’t backed by a campaign or a special interest group — are hard to come by. They would offer a different perspective, Elway said. Stuart Elway, a retired longtime independent pollster in Washington state, speaks to journalists ahead of the 2023 legislative session in Washington. (Photo courtesy of Stuart Elway) “An independent poll that’s not sponsored by any party or candidate or interest group gives you an objective measure of how the election is going, and I think more importantly, what the people are thinking about when they’re thinking about the election,” he said. Some polling experts say that Idaho lacks independent polls because the state is reliably Republican controlled, and independent pollsters aren’t willing to invest the high funds needed to conduct reliable polling. Instead, there are candidate and special interest groups polling in Idaho, like the back and forth of polls released by the campaigns of Risch and Achilles. The poll released last week by Achilles’ campaign, conducted by VoteNexus , had info on other races — including 54% opposition for Proposition 1, a ballot initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban. In other key races, like for governor, and two U.S. House seats, Republicans were in the lead. The survey, conducted via online polls sent by text message of 700 likely Idaho voters, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Idaho health officials on Tuesday reported the state’s second flu death in the 2026-27 influenza season. The death was of a resident of Elmore County, a rural area outside Boise, who was in their 80s, the regional health agency, Central District Health, announced. The first death, reported last week, was of an Owyhee County man who was older than age 65. The deaths come as public health officials say that influenza is spreading earlier in the year than usual. In recent weeks, emergency department and urgent care visits related to the flu have been higher than they were during the same time last year, state health officials say. Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Officials at Central District Health say vaccination is the best way to reduce the risk of severe flu illness. “While most people who get the flu recover without serious complications, some groups are at higher risk for severe illness, hospitalization, and death,” said Dr. Jaime Butler-Dawson, the health district’s epidemiology program manager. “These include adults age 65 and older, pregnant people, young children, people with obesity, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes, or kidney disease.” According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season. Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death. items.body: The College of Western Idaho says its first major fundraising campaign was a $33 million success. On Tuesday, CWI said its Powering the Treasure Valley campaign had exceeded its $30 million goal — funding capital projects and scholarships at the state’s largest community college. “This campaign has always been about our students,” CWI President Gordon Jones said in a news release Tuesday. “Every gift has helped create more opportunities for students to pursue an education, develop the skills employers need, and build a future close to home.” The campaign, launched in July 2023, will leave an imprint across CWI’s landscape. Money will go toward three capital projects on the Nampa campus: The campaign helped fund the Norco Health & Science Building and Agricultural Sciences Complex , which both opened in 2025, and the CapEd Student Success Center, a student services complex that opened earlier this year. Campaign funds will also go toward the CWI downtown Boise campus and the Micron Academic Center , which is expected to open in fall 2027. CWI says the campaign also supports student aid. Since the launch in 2023, CWI has increased its annual scholarship awards from $609,000 to more than $1 million this year. However, the completed fundraising campaign won’t support two other high-profile initiatives on CWI’s radar. This money will not go toward deferred maintenance on the recently acquired Ford Idaho Center , although college officials have said fundraising will be a component in covering the $25 million in maintenance costs. This money also will not go toward an endowment-based initiative to launch CWI’s first intercollegiate athletics programs. “When CWI launched Powering the Treasure Valley … we committed to two priorities: improving the student experience and adding capacity so we can serve more students,” college spokesman Ashley Smith said in a text Tuesday.

items.body: McMillan Elementary can serve 475 students, but just 171 students attend the school today. Enrollment has fallen by 62% since 2014. Class sizes are much smaller than the average across the West Ada School District. Some grade levels only have one class. Taxpayers are subsidizing the cost of heating and cooling empty rooms. The building needs $5.4 million in repairs and updates within 10 years. items.body: KUNA – The Kuna School District plans to recommend new guidance on student screen time before the end of the school year as leaders work to determine how much time students spend on computers and other devices, and what they’re doing on those devices. The effort stems from community concerns about too much student screen time, said Kuna Teaching and Learning Director Kevin Gifford. The nearby West Ada district launched a similar initiative in August. “The endgame ultimately is to have a district guidance document with clear goals for what we believe an appropriate balance of screen time would be,” Gifford said. In the meantime, the district has provided some immediate guidance for teachers. Kuna’s teacher guidance A guidance document Gifford distributed to district administrators and teachers provides three “best practices” to implement immediately: Ensure screen time is teacher-planned and directed to reduce “passive consumption.” Provide students with tech-free options during downtime. Collect data on how and when students use digital learning tools and applications. The district hasn’t collected data that clearly show how much time students spend on screens, Gifford told Idaho Education News. Still, national news coverage of instructional software i-Ready led to complaints in Kuna earlier this year, Gifford said. The new initiative to gather data and recommend new rules is, in part, to quell those concerns. Student screen time expanded during the COVID pandemic, when the district largely moved to online learning, putting students on Chromebooks at home. Six years later, district leaders wonder if they are properly balancing screen time with other activities in school. The district will begin measuring student device usage to create a live data report showing districtwide screen time averages. Gifford said the goal is to gather accurate and complete data to “tell the whole story, so that we’re not just reacting to perceptions.” Parts of the initiative start in the coming weeks. The district will guide teachers to ensure students have tech-free options during free time after completing assignments, during recess or between classes. Parents will receive a district survey asking for their opinions on device usage, but the district hasn’t determined when that will happen. Gifford feels the district is also getting ahead of the Legislature, where devices in schools have been a topic of discussion in recent years. In 2025, legislators unanimously approved a law directing school districts to limit students’ access to cellphones. In the 2026 session, lawmakers discussed artificial intelligence in schools but not screen time. Senate Bill 1227 directed the Idaho Department of Education to develop a framework for “responsible use” of AI in K-12 schools. Meanwhile, some educators are evaluating whether certain students should be on computers at all. Idaho Education Technology Association communications coordinator Will Goodman told EdNews in August that the organization plans to lobby for a ban on screens in kindergarten through third grade classrooms. “I know our Legislature is going to be looking at this very topic this year,” Gifford told Kuna trustees at the district’s October board meeting. “It’ll be good for us to be already working toward it.”

(Photo courtesy of the Idaho Family Policy Center) Opponents of the proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to pull TV ads paid for by the Idaho Democratic Party in favor of the initiative. The conservative, Christian advocacy organization, the Idaho Family Policy Center, and leaders with a political action committee that opposes the initiative, Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, brought the lawsuit. The ballot initiative Prop 1 would repeal Idaho’s abortion ban, allowing the procedure up to viability or after in cases of emergency, enumerate rights related to a range of reproductive healthcare, and provide legal liability protections for healthcare providers who provide that type of care. The initiative will be before Idaho voters in the Nov. 3 general election. The lawsuit, filed in Canyon County court, alleges that the supporters and authors of Prop 1, a group called Idahoans United for Women and Families, paid the Idaho Democratic Party to run ads in favor of the initiative in order to pay the more favorable rates that broadcasters are required to charge to political candidates ahead of elections. The ads were run on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens. “Pro-abortion activists cheated their way into cheaper television advertisements to stump for their radical abortion ballot initiative,” Idaho Family Policy Center President Blaine Conzatti said in a written statement. “Instead of playing by the rules of the game as outlined in our state campaign finance laws, Idahoans United for Women and Families colluded with the Idaho Democratic Party to mislead voters and gain an unfair advantage. Idaho voters deserve transparency — not shell games and dirty tricks.” Idaho Democratic Party spokesperson Avery Roberts called the lawsuit “frivolous” in an email to the Idaho Capital Sun. She said it was “another attempt by opponents of Prop 1 to distract from the devastating consequences of Idaho’s extreme abortion ban.” “Women are being forced to leave the state for lifesaving medical care, and the politicians responsible have done nothing to fix it,” Roberts said. “Instead of addressing the harm this ban has caused, opponents are trying to silence the families speaking out, even after the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed our advertising complies with Idaho campaign finance laws. We won’t be intimidated into silence. Idahoans deserve to hear these families’ stories and make up their own minds on November 3.” The family policy center helped author Idaho’s law allowing family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. Proposition 1, also called the Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act , also provides protections for access to birth control, in vitro fertilization and privacy in healthcare decisions. Chrissy Teigen (Photo courtesy of Chrissy Teigen) Teigen, who is a New York Times #1 bestselling cookbook author, model, entrepreneur and advocate for maternal health, will meet privately with Idaho mothers to talk with them about how the state’s abortion ban laws have affected them. She’ll then speak at a “Yes on Prop 1” rally, to be held from noon to 1 p.m. Wednesday at Treefort Music Hall, to encourage Idahoans to cast their ballots during the final days of early voting. The Treefort Music Hall is located at 722 W. Broad St. in Downtown Boise, and the rally is open to the public. Idahoans will decide the outcome of Proposition 1 during the Nov. 3 general election. It would take a simple majority of “yes” votes across the state to approve Prop 1. Under Idaho’s abortion ban laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors in Idaho can be sued for a minimum of $20,000 and be criminally prosecuted for performing an abortion. “In September 2020, Teigen underwent a medically necessary abortion at 20 weeks after experiencing a partial placental abruption, a serious pregnancy complication that put her health at risk,” a press release announcing Teigen’s appearance said. “The pregnancy was deeply wanted, but the baby was not expected to survive, and continuing the pregnancy posed serious risks to Teigen’s health.” Idaho’s abortion ban laws do not carve out an exception to protect a mother’s health, and instead only has an exception to prevent her death. items.body: A former teacher has sued the Boise School District, saying she was made the “fall guy” over a series of sexual abuse complaints. Marianne Baker is seeking at least $10,000 from the district. She says district officials forced her to resign from her special education job at Valley View Elementary School after she reported concerns about Gavin Snow, a paraprofessional who worked for Baker at Valley View. The district has agreed to $7 million in civil settlements to Boise parents who accused Snow of sexual abuse. “(Baker) was made the ‘fall guy’ for the district’s shortcomings and negligent hiring of Gavin Snow,” according to the Oct. 1 lawsuit. “Marianne was stripped of her professional passion and has suffered immense reputational damage that will follow her for the rest of her life.” District spokesman Dan Hollar declined to comment on the lawsuit Monday, because the case is “the subject of ongoing litigation.” The lawsuit presents a timeline of Baker’s final months with the Boise district: December 2024: On three occasions, Baker observes Snow had his phone in the bathroom while helping special education students — in violation of Baker’s policy for paraprofessionals. “Marianne assumed Gavin was being insubordinate by texting during working hours,” the lawsuit says. Jan. 6-7, 2025: Noting a change in Snow’s demeanor, Baker seeks to file a report with then-Valley View Principal Rick Jordan and other officials. Jan. 7, 2025: School counselor Paula Perry announces a new no-phones-in-bathrooms policy. After the meeting, Snow follows Baker into an empty staff room. Fearing for her safety, Baker leaves the room. “It was at that point that Marianne knew Gavin had done something nefarious and/or illegal with the children of her class,” the lawsuit says. Jan. 10, 2025: Jordan and a top district official tell Baker she had done the right thing by reporting Snow, the lawsuit says, “because the detectives had found child pornography on Gavin’s phone and computer at home.” About an hour after this conversation, Baker learns that Snow had taken his own life as Boise police tried to arrest him on child sexual abuse charges. Feb. 21, 2025: The district tells Baker that she is being placed on administrative leave for failing to report child abuse, abandonment or neglect. May 8, 2025: Boise Education Association leaders Lara Luthy and Stephanie Myers tell Baker that the district would be terminating her, giving her the option to resign and receive pay and benefits through September. “Lara and Stephanie informed Marianne that if she resigned, her employment file would be ‘cleaner’ and she would be able to seek employment in a school district elsewhere,” the lawsuit says. May 13, 2025: Baker “reluctantly” signs a letter of resignation. May 20, 2025: Boise district attorney Dan Skinner files a complaint against Baker with the Professional Standards Commission, a volunteer board that can revoke or suspend teaching certificates. June 16, 2025: Baker receives a criminal summons. She is charged with two misdemeanor counts of failing to report suspected abuse. Jan. 5: Magistrate Judge David Manweiler dismisses the misdemeanor counts . That same day, district officials uploaded the PSC complaint to her employment file. In her lawsuit, Baker says she has suffered high blood pressure and anxiety and “significant depression” due to the administrative leave and resignation. She says she now works as a flight attendant and a bartender on weekends, making “significantly less” than what she earned as a teacher. Baker filed a $1 million tort claim in November , as a precursor to the lawsuit.

items.body: An Ada County judge will privately review data spreadsheets compiled by Boise State University researchers before ruling on whether the university must hand them over to an anti-abortion lobbying group. The Idaho Family Policy Center (IFPC) — a Christian lobbying group that helped write Idaho’s restrictive abortion laws — sued Boise State , alleging that it withheld public records related to a widely cited article co-authored by two researchers affiliated with the university. The article said that obstetrician-gynecologists fled Idaho after the state’s abortion ban took effect in 2022. Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" class="size-full wp-image-127657" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" alt="" width="150" height="200" /> Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin In December, IFPC filed a records request seeking “all documents” and “all data” related to the article, but Boise State only provided a single, two-page spreadsheet. In a July petition to Ada County’s district court, IFPC argued that the research “must have produced a paper trail longer than two pages.” IFPC’s petition asked the court to compel the university to hand over additional records, including emails along with documents from Boise State’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), which approved the researchers’ process for collecting data on human subjects. District Judge Nancy Baskin heard arguments in the case Friday. Carsten Peterson, an attorney at Hawley Troxell, represented Boise State. While Peterson acknowledged that additional records related to the article exist, including various other data sets, he argued that the university reviewed IFPC’s request “in good faith” and provided the only record that matched its request. After asking the attorneys questions for more than an hour, Baskin ordered Boise State to show her any data files that the university deemed outside the scope of IFPC’s request. Baskin will review the spreadsheets “in-camera,” meaning behind closed doors, before she issues a written ruling on IFPC’s petition. Boise State has 10 days to deliver the spreadsheets to Baskin. Article heavily cited in debate over abortion laws The article, published last year by the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), reported that 35% of OB-GYNs left Idaho between 2022 and 2024 — after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, triggering Idaho’s abortion ban. Carsten Peterson, an attorney at Hawley Troxell, a private law firm representing Boise State. (Photo credit: Hawley Troxell) Two researchers affiliated with Boise State — J. Edward McEachern, an adjunct faculty member and doctor at St. Luke’s, and Allen Traylor, a graduate student — co-authored the article with a doctor unaffiliated with the university. They conducted three “ cross-sectional censuses” of OB-GYN physicians practicing obstetrics in Idaho to determine how many left the state after the U.S. Supreme Court decision. The article has been frequently cited in coverage detailing the effects of Idaho’s abortion ban, including by the New York Times last week, and by supporters of Proposition 1.
