(Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho lawmakers will weigh whether to fund several drug-prevention and treatment projects, totaling over $3 million, through the state’s endowment fund from tobacco lawsuit settlement money. The legislative Joint Millennium Fund Committee, which oversees the endowment, heard 10 proposals Friday for use of the settlement money, which must go toward drug and alcohol prevention. As of Sept. 30, the fund’s balance was nearly $43.5 million — however, some of the previously approved projects hadn’t yet been funded, according to Senior Budget and Policy Analyst Janica Bisharat. The committee is focused particularly on youth prevention and cessation in approving use of the fund for projects. Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, (right) chats with Sen. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle, on the Senate floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “I am laser-focused on prevention,” committee co-Chair Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, said Friday. “I have three deaths in my family already, and two or three more that are getting close. I’ve seen abuse. I’ve seen the problem, and as long as I have this position, I’m gonna focus on that. And that’s the focus of our group here is prevention.” The committee did not decide on its recommended projects to fund. The funding would need final approval from legislative budget writers on the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee during the legislative session, which begins in January. Here are the proposed projects lawmakers heard Friday: Recovery Idaho asks for $32,780 to create a certification process for recovery centers The nonprofit Recovery Idaho sought just under $33,000 to create a voluntary accreditation program for recovery centers statewide. Recovery centers provide treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and also often provide additional support for clients in treatment. “The problem right now is that the recovery community centers throughout the state are very well intentioned, but there’s a fair amount of variation and maybe not enough tracking of what exactly happens and what those outcomes are,” Andra Smith Hansen, a Recovery Idaho board member, told the committee members. Recovery centers provide support to adults, but many of those adults are parents, Smith Hansen said, and better outcomes for those adults can lead to better outcomes for their children. The money would be used to work with recovery centers statewide to develop standards, a process for accreditation and standardized metrics to evaluate outcomes. items.body: The Pocatello-Chubbuck School District will stick with a five-day school week and trimester schedule after trustees unanimously rejected proposals to adopt a four-day week and semesters. The vote happened at a board meeting Tuesday and follows months of consideration that fleshed out trustees’ preferences for keeping the district’s schedules intact . Trustees discussed a possible change to how the district uses Fridays, but the board took no action. Two trustees proposed exploring different hybrid models, but neither motion received a second. “We have a consensus that we certainly do want to look at the options,” said Board Chair Raymond Knoff. “It probably is too late for us to do that this year.” The change to a four-day week would have made Pocatello-Chubbuck one of the largest districts in Idaho to adopt the model. The similarly sized Nampa district made the switch two years ago. Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees each had their own concerns with the change. Trustee Megan Furniss cited concerns about a lack of input from the district’s families who qualify for free- and reduced-price lunch. Trustee Bill Osborn simply wanted to stay in line with most school districts in the country. “If it was such a good idea, why haven’t more school districts in the past five decades gone after it?” asked Osborn, echoing his statements at a recent meeting. Finances weren’t part of the five-day week or hybrid discussions. “In my opinion, it shouldn’t be part of the conversation,” said district business manager Jonathan Balls, “just because there’s a lot bigger factors out there than the finances.”

items.body: October is Dyslexia Awareness Month in Idaho, and over the past 10 years, Idaho professionals have prioritized early literacy and dyslexia education statewide. From updated, data-driven instruction for incoming teachers to intervention tutoring for elementary students, Boise State University has been at the forefront of these literacy initiatives. In September, Boise State University awarded its first endowed professorship in education to Clinical Associate Professor Carolyn Cort. Her specialty is early literacy. At BSU, Cort teaches courses in the early language and literacy endorsement, which is similar to a minor, for education majors and teacher candidates. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The director of Idaho’s largest state agency will step down by the end of the year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron told employees in a letter she’d be stepping back to provide more support to her family, Boise State Public Radio first reported. Gov. Brad Little’s communication director, Emily Callihan, told BSPR that Charron’s father faced “significant health challenges.” “This has not been an easy decision,” Charron wrote in the letter to employees. “The past year has brought significant challenges for my family, and I realize that they need more of my time, attention, and support. Family has always been important to me, and right now, being there for mine needs to be my priority.” Charron’s last day has not been finalized, and it’s unclear who will serve as interim director when she leaves. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Little appointed Charron as director in July 2025, and she officially stepped into the post in September last year, after previously serving as the agency’s top Medicaid official since 2021, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. “I want to thank Juliet Charron for her outstanding service as Health and Welfare Director,” Little said in a written statement to the Sun. “Under her leadership, the department made meaningful progress in strengthening child welfare prevention, preparing to distribute nearly $200 million in Rural Health Transformation funding in the coming months as part of nearly $1 billion over five years, and improving compliance, accountability, and program outcomes. I appreciate her commitment to serving Idahoans and look forward to announcing new leadership for the state’s largest agency before the end of the year.” Health and Welfare spokesman AJ McWhorter told the Sun the agency had “a number of vacancies in some key positions for a variety of unrelated reasons, including external opportunities, retirements, and personal and family reasons.” “The Governor’s Office will announce a new director at a later date,” McWhorter said. “DHW is hiring for the other positions, and we encourage qualified people to apply. items.body: How much growth is too much, and too fast? The State Board of Education grappled with that question last week, and couldn’t wrestle it into submission. The board punted on a three-year plan that guides new growth and new programs at the state’s colleges and universities. In its stead, the board gave the schools a one-year go-ahead, enough to let them keep working on new programs for 2027-28. The three-year plan is on hold until the board’s December meeting. Yes, three-year plans are wonky and boring. Until you think about what’s being planned. If you’re a taxpayer, here’s why you ought to care. The whole idea behind the three-year plan is to grow the higher education portfolio in an orderly way — without wasting tax dollars on redundant programs. If you’re student, or soon to be one, here’s why you ought to care. These plans will help determine what you can study, and where, laying out your options for career credentials or a full-blown degree. And if you’re an employer, here’s why you ought to care. Many of the new additions to the three-year plans focus on the state’s hottest job sectors — such as healthcare and cybersecurity. These are the new programs Idaho employers need: pipelines from the campus to the workplace. So the State Board is debating something that sounds dull, but is actually crucial. Who wants what? items.body: Vallivue School District trustees cured two open meeting violations from a meeting last week, appointed a trustee to fill one vacancy and asked the Canyon County Board of Commissioners to fill a second vacancy, as required by law if a board fails to fill a vacancy after 120 days. Trustees appointed Kellie Horrocks at a special meeting Wednesday. The mother of four young children is the new trustee for Zone 4 and replaces Paul Tierney, who resigned in August . Horrocks joined Wednesday’s meeting by phone. “Truth be told, I don’t know a lot about what goes on on the board,” Horrocks said in her interview. Two other candidates — Idaho Power attorney Brian Bishop and restaurant assistant manager Esther Ma, who is also running for the State Senate as a Constitution Party candidate in District 11 — attended in person. “The types of things that the board does are things I do every day in my work,” Bishop said in his interview. Click to view slideshow. Board Chair Jennifer Cox said she liked that Horrocks has young children, bringing a different perspective to the board, and is willing to learn. “She was off-the-hip honest,” Cox said. After conducting the three interviews, trustees deliberated in open session then voted unanimously to appoint Horrocks, which was noticed on the agenda as an action item. Last week, the board handled a vacancy in Zone 3 differently. Resolving open meeting violations The board last week interviewed two candidates to fill the vacancy in Zone 3, left by trustee Toni Brinegar, who resigned in June . Trustees then deliberated and came to a “consensus” to appoint naturopathic medical doctor Brett Butterfield, but the meeting’s agenda did not include an action item to make the appointment. After that meeting, EdNews emailed district leaders to express concerns regarding possible open meeting violations. “Thank you for your patience and thank you for bringing your concerns to our attention,” Finance Director Dalelyn Allen responded last Thursday. items.summary: Trained teachers and staff will carry guns in Marsing and Homedale schools after trustees in both districts unanimously approved policies last week. The policies are all identical, word-for-word, except for the districts’ names. “This Policy is only to aid Homedale School Distri
items.body: Trained teachers and staff will carry guns in Marsing and Homedale schools after trustees in both districts unanimously approved policies last week. The armed staff policies are modeled after one in the Kimberly School District , which rolled out its program last year. The policies are all identical, word-for-word, except for the districts’ names. “This Policy is only to aid Homedale School District in deterring, detecting, and denying some type of active shooter incident from occurring on school property,” Homedale’s policy reads. Approved staff members carrying a firearm will “be responsible to defend, using deadly force, if necessary, their zone of responsibility.” The Homedale and Marsing school boards must now approve individual staff members to carry a concealed firearm on campus. Criteria for approval include: Possession of a current Idaho Enhanced Concealed Weapon License A recommendation from the superintendent A physical and psychological assessment The board can deny permission for any reason and will review staff members’ grants of permission annually. Once approved, employees must complete at least 40 hours of training. “Training will include engagement on the range with a certified instructor in live fire situations that require ‘shoot, don’t shoot’ decision making and other dynamic scenarios,” the policy says. District leaders said they heard mostly positive feedback from community members. “Every community member that I’ve talked to … has been super positive, saying we should’ve done this years ago,” Marsing Board Chair Jason Sevy told Idaho Education News. On Monday, after approving the policy, Homedale held a community meeting to gather feedback. Dwayne Fisher told EdNews he only heard positive feedback. Trustees in both districts had been considering the policy for years. Marsing surveyed its employees in 2022 but didn’t act until this year. Days after both districts approved their policies, a school shooter killed four people at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon. Megan Lambert , a Boise State University graduate and special education teacher, died in the shooting. “W ith what just happened in Bend, u nfortunately, it’s on the forefront of everyone’s minds again,” Fisher said. “More than anything, we’re hoping that people know our schools are not going to be soft targets.” Both districts have begun installing signs showing that staff members may be armed.

(Photo by Gregory Thomas/USDA) High costs and lengthy permitting processes are two of the barriers to bringing nuclear-powered electricity to customers in Idaho, officials from three electrical utilities told state regulators during a public forum outside of Boise on Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios. However, the high cost to build nuclear power projects, the absence of price certainty and permitting processes that can stretch for 10 years or longer do not align with state regulators’ “least cost, least risk” mandate. “When I think of the benefits of nuclear, I think diversity is a huge part of it,” Idaho Power Chief Operating Officer Adam Richins said. “Obviously, it’s dispatchable clean energy, which really doesn’t exist besides nuclear.” Adam Richins was named Idaho Power’s executive vice president and chief operating officer in February 2026 after previously serving in other roles at the utility. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Power) “On the other side of the spectrum … right now we don’t know how much it’s going to cost, and obviously when you talk about ‘least cost, least risk,’ that is very important,” Richins said. For example, Richins said the expansion of Plant Vogtle nuclear power plant in Georgia ran over budget by $16 billion to $21 billion. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission sets rates and regulates investor-owned and privately-owned utilities that provide electricity, gas, water or some telephone services for a profit. The three members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, or PUC for short, are appointed by the governor. None of the three companies use nuclear in their energy mix. But Rocky Mountain Power officials recently announced a 40-year power purchase agreement to buy electricity from a TerraPower nuclear power plant that is being built in Kemmerer, Wyoming. The Wyoming plant is being built at the site of a coal plant that is being retired, with about $2 billion in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Energy supporting the project. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission did not have any specific nuclear energy proposals under consideration during Tuesday’s forum and did not take any action. “The primary purpose of this opportunity for us is to listen to each and every one (of the utilities participating in the forum),” Idaho PUC Chairman Edward Lodge said. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In the race for Idaho’s top election official, two familiar names are headed to the ballot. Democratic challenger Shawn Keenan is again challenging Republican incumbent Secretary of State Phil McGrane , who widely defeated Keenan in the 2022 election. Keenan, a mortgage broker and loan officer who lives in Coeur d’Alene, says he’s running again to avoid and combat election misinformation. McGrane, a seasoned Idaho election official seeking a second term, says he’s running on a track record of keeping elections secure and improving access to election information. The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. The secretary of state is a statewide office that oversees elections in the state, manages campaign finance compliance and transparency, and maintains records on businesses. The secretary of state also serves on the Land Board, which manages the state’s endowment lands. The secretary of state serves a four-year term and earns an annual salary of $128,690. In a Republican-controlled state, Keenan’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. Educational exhibits are placed along the trail to provide information. (Photo courtesy of the National Park Service) The Friends of Minidoka nonprofit will host its 2026 symposium, which will feature a film screening, legal discussion and lecture, “to consider the enduring importance of due process, equal protection, and civic engagement in protecting our civil liberties and strengthening democracy,” according to a press release from the organization. The 2026 Civil Liberties Symposium, titled Law, Civil Liberties, and the Continuing Pursuit of Justice: From Wayne Collins to Today, will examine how “the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II continues to inform contemporary debates surrounding immigration, detention, national security, and constitutional rights,” the press release said. In 1942, the Minidoka War Relocation Center was constructed in Jerome County at Hunt, Idaho. Locally, it was known as “Hunt Camp.” While in operation, the site was the seventh largest city in Idaho, incarcerating nearly 9,400 people at its peak population. (Photo courtesy of the National Archives and Records Administration) The series begins Thursday with a screening of “Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman,” a 30-minute documentary about the San Francisco attorney who spent more than two decades defending Japanese Americans who renounced their U.S. citizenship under duress while imprisoned at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II. The screening will be followed by a discussion with Emily Croston, staff attorney with the ACLU of Idaho, and Wendy Olson, former U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho and chairwoman of the Idaho State Bar’s Diversity Section. On Nov. 5, the group will host its 2026 distinguished lecture: “Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do,” presented by Kari Hong, the director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law. Drawing on her experience as an immigration attorney, public interest lawyer, and legal scholar, Hong will examine the history and present-day realities of immigration enforcement and detention, along with opportunities to protect the rights of affected individuals. The lecture will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the audience. The symposium concludes Dec. 8 with an online presentation of Hong’s distinguished lecture, offering another opportunity for community members to participate and engage with these issues. “History reminds us that civil liberties can be threatened when fear and claims of national security are used to justify the erosion of constitutional protections,” said Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka. “By bringing historical perspectives into conversation with today’s legal challenges, the Civil Liberties Symposium creates opportunities for our community to learn, ask difficult questions, and consider our shared responsibility to uphold justice.” All events are free and open to the public, with registration required. items.body: An orange "detour ahead" sign alerts motorists of a new route around new housing construction in Boise in summer 2026. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s newly approved Opportunity Zones could help bring more housing, businesses and jobs to communities across the state. The attraction for investors is the potential tax savings. This month, Idaho Commerce announced that the U.S. Treasury approved 25 zones, including areas in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls. The new Opportunity Zone designations take effect Jan. 1. An Opportunity Zone is a designated area where the federal government offers tax benefits to encourage private investment. The idea is straightforward: give investors a financial reason to put money into communities that could benefit from more economic activity. In Boise, the five areas identified by the city are Downtown, Shoreline, University District, South Boise Village and West Boise . These are general descriptions of the selected areas. The actual boundaries determine whether a particular property is included. In North Idaho, the officially designated list includes parts of Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls, as well as areas around Blanchard and Kellogg, Smelterville and Wardner. Other designated communities include Caldwell, Garden City, Nampa, Pocatello and Twin Falls. The state’s announcement provides the complete list and a link to look up the boundaries . The program connects investors with projects that need money. An investor who sells stock, real estate or a business at a profit may face a tax bill on that gain. By investing an eligible gain through a special investment vehicle called a Qualified Opportunity Fund, the investor may receive tax benefits. The fund puts that money into qualifying property or businesses within a zone. The IRS explains the basic structure here . Imagine a business owner who sells a company and wants to invest some of the profit. Across town, a developer wants to turn an underused property into apartments with shops on the ground floor. If the project is in an Opportunity Zone and meets the program’s requirements, an Opportunity Fund could connect that investor’s money with the development. The investor receives an ownership interest, and the project receives money to help move forward. Under the new rules beginning in 2027, a qualifying investor generally can delay tax on the invested gain for five years and reduce the amount of that gain subject to tax. Holding the investment for at least 10 years may also allow the investor to avoid federal tax on qualifying growth in the investment’s value. Coeur d’Alene also offers a potential partnership story. Idaho Capital Sun reported that Kootenai County and the Coeur d’Alene Tribe both sought designation for the local tract. The application summary identified vacant tribal land as an opportunity for investment involving the Tribe, local governments, and private developers. That possibility deserves attention, although the designation itself does not establish a finalized development partnership. For investors, those benefits can make a long-term investment more attractive. For developers and business owners, the program can help attract money from people willing to wait for a project to mature. That could support a new apartment building, the redevelopment of an older commercial property, or the expansion of a qualifying business. Residents may benefit from additional homes, employment, and services. Those outcomes are possibilities, not promises. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: Work continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, on April 17, 2026. Today’s data center buildout has become the largest industrial boom since the railroad era of the 19th century, with $10 trillion in investment and almost twice the economic impact. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) The sheer size of investment in data centers is drawing concern as it surpasses all other historical booms and crowds out other more job-creating ventures. Until now, no industry had driven the U.S. economy with such force since the railroad expansion of the late 1800s, when titans battled one another to lay the transcontinental tracks that would connect America from coast to coast. Railroads in the 19 th century consumed about $173 billion in today’s dollars and created more than 2% of the nation’s annual economic output (GDP) over 20 years. Today’s data center buildout will dwarf that amount, with $10 trillion in investment, and now have almost twice the economic impact — nearly 4% of GDP. That’s according to a report created by a Columbia Business School professor, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. States are starting to feel left out of the windfall, many having granted tax exemptions before the boom. Years ago, before artificial intelligence prompted a tsunami of building, states typically welcomed data centers supporting internet traffic, offering tax abatements and other perks. Many officials now are rethinking that approach as tax revenues take a bigger hit and high energy demands take a toll on affordability. Nevada , for instance, trimmed tax abatements and will ask data centers to agree to foot the bill for energy and water demands, in a September executive order from Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. States where data center costs will be concentrated over the three years are Texas ($638 billion), Virginia ($249 billion), Ohio ($169 billion) and Georgia ($160 billion), according to projections from Industrial Info Resources, a market intelligence firm. Southern states dominate the landscape for the number of data centers planned, with large numbers also proposed in Arizona, California, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington state, according to a Pew Research Center report in April. The profitability of AI has yet to catch up with the expense of the buildout. “It is not a pretty picture right now,” said IIR’s senior vice president of research, David Pickering. “I think it will become profitable once things settle down a bit and more legislation is put in place to regulate how we handle AI. “The big players will no doubt find a way to make it profitable,” he said. There are signs the staggering cost of data centers is crowding out other investments such as housing. Over the past two years new construction value for data centers has more than doubled to $85 billion annually, while all other construction value has dropped 8%, according to a Stateline analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data as of August. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s newly refurbished replica of the Liberty Bell will be rededicated Nov. 23 during ceremonies at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise, Idaho State Historical Society Executive Director Janet Gallimore said Thursday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE In January, the bell was sent to the Bell Foundry Christoph in Charleston, S.C. for cleaning and refurbishing in connection with this year’s America250 celebrations in Idaho. The refurbished Liberty Bell made it back to the Idaho State Capitol in July for the America250 celebration, and then was sent on a tour of cities and towns in all 44 Idaho counties so that school children and the public could see and ring the bell. At the completion of the statewide tour, the Liberty Bell will return to Boise for a free, public rededication ceremony at noon on Nov. 23. During those ceremonies, the Liberty Bell will be reinstalled at its home on the front steps of the Idaho State Capitol. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US The America250 in Idaho Advisory Council in December voted to spend up to $28,500 to clean and refurbish the Liberty Bell. During the America250 in Idaho Advisory Council’s meeting on Thursday, Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth floated the idea of installing a new liberty fountain in Idaho as a permanent landmark for this year’s America250 celebration. Ellsworth, who said she has already had Zoom meetings with state legislators on the subject, estimated the liberty fountain would cost $1 million, and encouraged the state to fundraise to generate the money for the fountain. “This is the gift that we want to give a lasting legacy to Idaho about America250,” Ellsworth said. Ellsworth did not say where the liberty fountain might be built. The advisory council did not take any action on the liberty fountain Thursday, but members encouraged Ellsworth to see if all the different officials and stakeholders who would need to support the project are on board and then report back during the council’s next meeting, which is tentatively scheduled for Dec. 10.

items.body: A volunteer helps a young person fill out a form on National Voter Registration Day in 2025. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue, but for many others it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. (Photo courtesy of Alliance for Youth Action) Editor’s Note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th . Boise State University senior Cade Syvock opposes abortion. As president of the school’s chapter of the conservative group Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late activist Charlie Kirk, Syvock helped coordinate anti-abortion protests on campus. But he’s not spending much time this fall campaigning against an Idaho ballot initiative that would restore abortion access. Not for lack of interest — he calls the proposed law “very, very extreme” because it allows abortions after viability in certain emergency cases — but because of pressing economic issues he’d rather be working on. “It’s not like everybody’s going out and getting abortions 24/7, but everybody is trying to find a home,” Syvock said. In Idaho and Missouri, where voters will decide the future of abortion access on Nov. 3, campaigns are trying to reach a generation dealing with rising living costs and skepticism toward politics. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue. But for many others, it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. Idaho’s initiative would restore abortion access. Missouri’s measure seeks to reinstate a near-total ban jettisoned by voters two years ago. People pushing for and against both measures are making their appeals to young voters, using social media and canvassing to increase turnout on Election Day, but they’re competing against other issues for Generation Z’s attention. “I’m not saying that the abortion stuff is any less important than housing, but I think in terms of what young people are focusing on right now, it’s definitely dropped a little bit,” Syvock said. Gen Z politicians who want to make a change grapple with parties that aren’t always ready for them In most elections, it’s difficult for campaigns to achieve high turnout among young voters, especially in between presidential election cycles. Less than half of the 40 million Gen Z Americans between ages 18 and 29 who were eligible to vote in 2024 cast a ballot, a study by the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University found. This year, the number of eligible Gen Z-age voters is estimated at nearly 50 million. But there are some signs that turnout could be higher this year. Nonpartisan youth vote organization The Civics Center noted a significant increase in voter registration among 18-year-olds compared with the 2022 midterms, from 35% to 42%. And the Tufts survey points out that there are many signs Gen Z is active and engaged on political subjects, but that connecting issues to candidates and ballot questions is the challenge. The majority of Gen Z adults support abortion access, according to a September poll from The 19th and YouGov. But there’s a gender gap: Women were more likely than men to say abortion should be always or mostly legal, 69% to 51%. Almost half of men versus 31% of women say it should be mostly or always illegal. The number of Generation Z Missourians who got involved in the 2024 initiative petition is not available, but more than 110,000 Idahoans signed the petition to put abortion access on the state ballot. About 7% of those signatures came from people between the ages of 18 and 25, and twice as many of those signatures came from women than from men. But some organizing efforts are made more difficult by local politics as well as increasing costs for food, housing and transportation. The 19th/YouGov poll found that 21% of Gen Z adults were worried about their ability to pay for groceries and 34% were somewhat worried. items.body: Voters cast their ballots during the May 19, 2026, primary election at The Waterfront in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman says she has a long track record of being a straightforward attorney who is running to keep politicization out of the office — something she says her opponent hasn’t done. But Raúl Labrador , the Republican incumbent running for a second term, says he transformed the office for the better — pointing to his legal victories defending state laws in court — in part because he followed through on a promise he made when he first campaigned: being an aggressive attorney general. The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. The attorney general is an elected office that serves as the state’s top attorney, which includes defending the state and its laws in court, and serves on the Idaho Land Board, which manages state endowment lands. The attorney general serves a four-year term and receives an annual salary of $146,730. In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. The state last had a Democratic attorney general more than 30 years ago. Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman speaks at a press conference announcing her endorsements on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Hickman, 61, is an Idaho attorney with two decades of experience, including at global tech company Micron and as a clerk in Idaho’s federal courthouse, the U.S. District Court for the District of Idaho. She hasn’t run for public office before. She spent her childhood moving around the country as part of a military family. She said she has lived for 30 years in Idaho, where she said her family has deep roots. In 2013, she joined the Boise-based law firm McFarland Ritter as an attorney focusing on business negotiation and litigation. She served as board chair for Mormon Women for Ethical Government, a nonpartisan and 501(c)(4) faith-based nonprofit organization that joined a lawsuit unsuccessfully challenging an Idaho law that established tax credits for students to attend private, religious schools. Hickman said the people she encountered in her involvement in that group encouraged her to run for the attorney general’s office. Though she’s running as a Democrat, she says she wishes the race was nonpartisan, like elections for judges in Idaho. “A good attorney just follows the law, wherever it goes,” Hickman said in a recent interview. Before filing to run, she said she was a registered Republican so she could vote in the state’s closed GOP primary elections. But Hickman said she joined the race as a Democrat because she felt she didn’t have enough time to gather 1,000 signatures to run as an independent, or to mount a competitive campaign for the Republican primary election in May, where Labrador ran unopposed. The Times and other national reports identified LaCivita as the co-manager of President Donald Trump’s 2024 election campaign and a senior adviser to the MAGA Inc. super PAC. While LaCivita is more well-known for his work for Trump and MAGA Inc., he has also worked in Idaho. In February, Little announced that LaCivita joined the Brad Little for Governor campaign as a senior adviser. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. I am glad to have him on the team.” Efforts to reach LaCivita this week were unsuccessful. Little’s campaign manager, Joan Vargas, did not respond to multiple requests from the Idaho Capital Sun asking if LaCivita still serves as a senior adviser to Little, and whether Little knew about the trip. Back when he joined Little’s campaign in February, LaCivita issued a written statement saying he was excited to help Little get re-elected in Idaho. “Joining the Brad Little for Governor campaign is a great honor and opportunity,” LaCivita said. “Gov. Little has been delivering results for Idahoans, and he is just getting started. I look forward to working with his team to keep Idaho one of the best states in the country.” It was not immediately clear what work LaCivita did for Little’s campaign or if LaCivita still serves as a senior adviser on Little’s campaign. In its story, the New York Times said it is common for political consultants to also work with foreign candidates and governments. However, the New York Times said LaCivita’s trip to Republika Srpska was notable because it occurred while LaCivita is working to help Trump-aligned candidates in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
